question: Which ILS limitation was MLS designed to overcome?

options.text: Only 40 channels worldwide
Interference from sky waves at night
No vertical guidance on the approach
No identification of the facility

explanation: ILS has only 40 channels, fixed narrow beams that force aircraft into one long sequence, no special procedures for slow aircraft or helicopters, and needs large flat cleared sites free of reflecting objects.

question: Why do ILS's fixed, narrow beams cause landing delays?

options.text: They limit all ILS approaches to Category I minima only
Every aircraft is sequenced onto one path
They cannot be received above 2 000 ft
They can be used only by aircraft with autoland

explanation: With one straight-in path, every arrival must be sequenced and separated along it. MLS allows curved and offset approaches, increasing runway use.

question: Why is ILS difficult to install in hilly areas?

options.text: Its VHF signals cannot cross hills
Its glide path angle cannot exceed 3°
Its markers need a flat site to be heard by the aircraft
It needs large areas of flat, clear ground

explanation: The localizer and glide path rely on the ground in front of the aerials. Uneven terrain and obstacles bend the beams, so ILS needs a large, flat, cleared site.

question: How many channels does MLS provide?
explanation: MLS has 200 channels worldwide, compared with ILS's 40.

question: In which band does MLS operate?

options.text: SHF, about 5 031 to 5 091 MHz
UHF, about 329 to 335 MHz
UHF, 962 to 1 213 MHz
VHF, 108 to 111.975 MHz

explanation: MLS works at about 5 GHz in the SHF band. The short wavelength lets the beams be narrow and makes siting far less critical.

question: What is MLS's minimum azimuth coverage either side of the runway on-course line?
explanation: Approach azimuth coverage is at least ±40° of the runway centre line, against the localizer's narrow course.

question: What range of glide slopes can be selected with MLS?

options.text: 3° only

explanation: Any glide slope between 0.9° and 20° can be selected, which suits helicopters and STOL aircraft as well as airliners.

question: What is the usable range of MLS in the UK?

options.text: 40 NM
10 NM
25 NM
20 NM

explanation: MLS is usable to 20–30 NM from the site; 20 NM in the UK.

question: What guidance does the MLS back azimuth provide?

options.text: Distance information to the far end of the runway
Glide slope guidance for the missed approach climb
Go-around and departure guidance, ±20°
Approach guidance to the reciprocal runway, with reversed sense

explanation: The back azimuth gives go-around and departure guidance within ±20° of runway direction, up to 15° elevation, 10 NM and 10 000 ft. MLS has no back-course problem.

question: Why are reflections from vehicles and buildings much less of a problem for MLS than ILS?

options.text: Its signals are horizontally polarized
It switches off whenever a vehicle enters the area
It uses a lower frequency that passes through obstacles
Its scanning beam lets reflections be rejected

explanation: The narrow, time-referenced scanning beam lets the system reject reflected signals, so beam bending by aircraft, vehicles and buildings is no longer a problem. Hilly sites need no levelling.

question: How does MLS provide range information?

options.text: By a DME, built into the system
By a co-located locator NDB
By timing the scanning beams
By three marker beacons at fixed points

explanation: MLS has a built-in DME instead of markers. For Cat II and III a precision DME (DME/P) accurate to within about 100 ft is required.

question: How accurate must a precision DME (DME/P) be for MLS Cat II and III approaches?

options.text: Within about 0.25 NM
Within about 100 ft
Within about 1 NM
Within about 10 ft

explanation: DME/P must be accurate to within roughly 100 ft to support Cat II and III MLS approaches, segmented and curved paths.

question: How is an MLS identified?

options.text: The letter M followed by two letters
Three letters with no prefix
A continuous tone
The letter I followed by two letters

explanation: MLS idents begin with M followed by two letters. ILS idents usually begin with I.

question: Which statement about MLS compatibility is correct?

options.text: It cannot drive the autopilot
It can be used only with an EFIS fitted
It needs a completely separate cockpit display for each pilot
It drives ILS-type displays, autopilots and RNAV

explanation: MLS outputs can drive conventional localizer and glide path displays, EFIS, autopilots and area navigation equipment.

question: To what standard are all MLS-equipped aircraft intended to operate?

options.text: Category II
Category I
Category III
Non-precision only

explanation: The aim is for all MLS-equipped aircraft to operate to Cat III criteria.

question: How does MLS share one frequency among its azimuth, elevation and data transmissions?

options.text: Each function uses a different modulation tone
Time division multiplexing on one frequency
Each function uses a separate paired frequency
Each function uses a different polarization on the same carrier

explanation: All transmissions share one frequency on a channel, but are synchronised to take turns — time division multiplexing — so they never interfere.

question: What principle does MLS use to measure azimuth and elevation?

options.text: Time-referenced scanning beam (TRSB)
Difference in depth of modulation of two lobes
Phase comparison of two 30 Hz signals
Pulse ranging from a ground transponder

explanation: A narrow beam sweeps to and fro (or up and down) at a constant rate. The aircraft measures the time between the two passes of the beam.

question: How does an MLS receiver find its azimuth angle?

options.text: From the DME range and the glide slope
From the strength of the received azimuth signal
From the phase difference of two reference signals
From the time between the "to" and "fro" sweeps

explanation: The beam sweeps across at uniform speed and back again. The interval between receiving the "to" and "fro" sweeps is proportional to the aircraft's angle from the centre line.

question: How does an MLS receiver find its elevation angle?

options.text: From the difference in depth of 90 Hz and 150 Hz signals
From the strength of the elevation signal
From the time between the up and down sweeps
From the DME range alone

explanation: A separate beam scans up and down at uniform speed; the time between the two passes gives the elevation angle, compared with the glide slope selected.

question: What does the pilot set to fly an offset MLS approach?

options.text: The back azimuth instead of the approach azimuth
An azimuth offset from the runway direction
The DME/P range to the start of the offset
A different localizer frequency for each offset

explanation: The pilot can fly the runway on-course line or select an approach azimuth a chosen number of degrees either side of it, and a required glide slope.

question: What is the status of the MLS flare elevation function?

options.text: Used only by helicopters
Standardised but not intended for implementation
Replaced by the back azimuth function
Required for all Category III operations

explanation: Although a flare elevation function was standardised, it is not planned to be implemented.

question: Which auxiliary data does MLS transmit?

options.text: Traffic information on other approaching aircraft
Glide path angles for all runways at the airfield
Aircraft position reports to ATC
Station ident, system and runway condition, weather

explanation: The data words carry station identification, system condition, runway condition and weather information.

question: What do the MLS cockpit cross bars show?

options.text: Deviation from the selected course and slope
Deviation from the runway centre line only
The bearing and distance of the MLS site
The aircraft's distance to touchdown and its ground speed

explanation: The display looks like an ILS display, but deviation is shown relative to the course and glide slope the pilot has selected.

question: What ground equipment is needed for curved or segmented MLS approaches?

options.text: A locator at the outer marker
A second azimuth transmitter
A precision DME (DME/P)
A VOR on the extended centre line

explanation: Segmented and curved approaches are computed using range, so a DME/P must be installed on the ground.

question: Why do aircraft often have multi-mode receivers?

options.text: To replace the radio altimeter
To receive ILS, MLS and GPS from one unit
To receive VOR and ADF on a single frequency
To combine the transponder and the DME in one box and aerial

explanation: A multi-mode receiver with a combined control unit handles ILS, MLS and GNSS approaches, easing crew workload.
